definitions.definition: The Saṃhitās speak of a One behind the many: That One which breathed windless by its own power before creation (RV 10.129.2), the One Being the inspired call by many names (1.164.46), the One that has become all this (8.58.2), the one-alone god in whom the gods become one (AVŚ 13.4), the Unborn that propped apart the six regions (RV 1.164.6), of whom there is no likeness (VS 32.3).

relations.note: The One is spoken of both as beyond the gods (10.129.6: the gods are later) and as what the gods' names name (1.164.46).

name: The gods as names of the One

definitions.definition: Several hymns hold that the many gods are names or forms of one: 'they call it Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni … the One Being the inspired speak of in many ways' (RV 1.164.46); the poets shape the one bird into many with words (10.114.5); 'great is the one asura-ship of the gods' (3.55); the one name-giver of the gods (10.82.3); 'that is Agni, that the Sun … that brahman' (VS 32.1). Yāska: the one Self of the deity is praised in many ways, the other gods are its limbs (Nirukta 7.4). The liturgy nonetheless addresses each god as a distinct recipient.

relations.note: The names-of-the-One teaching is one aspect of the Saṃhitās' teaching on the One.

notes: The modern labels 'henotheism/kathenotheism' are scholarly metadata and not used here.

definitions.definition: In the Ṛgveda brahman is the potent formulation and prayer (its lord is Bṛhaspati); in the Atharvaveda and White Yajurveda it becomes the name of the highest: 'homage to the highest Brahman' (AVŚ 10.8.1), 'those who know Brahman in man know the Supreme' (10.7.17), Brahman entered the golden city of the body (10.2.33), 'that is brahman' (VS 32.1), 'Oṃ, the void is brahman' (VS 40.17).

relations.note: The Skambha hymn identifies the frame of the world with the highest Brahman.

definitions.definition: The thousand-headed Person who is all this, past and future, of whom one quarter is all beings and three quarters the immortal in heaven; sacrificed by the gods, he became the world, the Vedas, the varṇas, sun, moon and gods (RV 10.90); 'knowing him alone one goes beyond death' (VS 31.18).

relations.note: One of the Saṃhitās' creation accounts.
The four varṇas are said to come from the Person's mouth, arms, thighs and feet.

definitions.definition: The Golden Germ who arose in the beginning as the one lord of what exists, giver of self and strength, whose shadow is immortality and death; born from the great waters; named Prajāpati (RV 10.121); Prajāpati moves unborn in the womb and is born in many ways (VS 31.19).

relations.note: One of the Saṃhitās' creation accounts.

name: Skambha, the frame of the world

definitions.definition: The pillar or frame in which tapas, ṛta, vows, faith and truth abide and on which the worlds rest; identified with the highest Brahman to which homage is paid (AVŚ 10.7–8); cf. the One that propped apart the six regions (RV 1.164.6).
The remainder of the sacrifice praised as the ground in which name and form, the world, the gods and the rites rest (AVŚ 11.7).

The vow-bound wanderer of Atharvaveda 15 who stirs Prajāpati into creation, becomes the one, the great, brahman, tapas and truth, becomes Mahādeva and Īśāna, stands upright a year, is seated on a throne of seasons and Vedas, has seven prāṇas identified with fire, sun, moon, wind, waters, animals and creatures, and is to be honoured above the king when he comes as guest.

names.name: Rudra, Tryambaka, Paśupati, Bhava, Śarva, Nīlagrīva, Śiva (epithet)

definitions.definition: Rudra is feared as the archer whose wrath and arrows harm men and cattle and is begged to turn them away, and loved as the best of physicians with a thousand remedies and a healing hand; he is lord of cattle (Paśupati), Bhava and Śarva, blue-necked; the Śatarudrīya pays homage to him as present in all places, beings and callings and names his auspicious, non-terrible body (śivā tanūḥ) and him as 'śiva, śivatara'; the Keśin drank with him from the cup.

name: Agni, the fire in the rite and in all

definitions.definition: Agni is the household priest, messenger and mouth of the gods who carries the oblation (RV 1.1), churned by Atharvan (6.16.13), guardian of ṛta, present as the flesh-eating and the oblation-bearing fire (10.16.9), as Vaiśvānara the light set in the heart (6.9).

Soma is the plant pressed in the sacrifice, the exhilarating drink that makes the drinkers say 'we have become immortal, we have gone to the light' (RV 8.48.3), the god purifying himself through the filter (book 9), bringer of bliss (9.113.6); set in heaven by ṛta (10.85.1).

relations.note: The Ṛgveda itself distinguishes the pressed plant from the soma the brahmins know (10.85.3).

definitions.definition: 'One thinks he has drunk soma when they crush the plant; the soma the brahmins know, of that no one eats' (RV 10.85.3); only the 'cooked' by tapas attain Soma's filter (9.83.1).

relations.note: An instance of the ritual substance understood beyond its outer form.

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu measured the worlds in three strides; his highest step, where there is a well-spring of honey and where god-seekers rejoice, the wise ever see like an eye stretched in heaven (RV 1.22.20, 1.154).
Indra, strengthened by soma, slays the serpent Vṛtra who enclosed the waters, releasing them and becoming king of what moves and rests (RV 1.32).

Māyā is the wondrous, creative or cunning power of a god: by it Varuṇa measured out the earth (RV 5.85.5), Indra goes in many forms (6.47.18); the wise see the bird anointed with the asura's māyā with heart and mind (10.177.1).

Virāj, born from the Puruṣa and giving birth to him (RV 10.90.5), was all this in the beginning and entered the fires, the assembly and the council; gods, men and others milked their foods from her (AVŚ 8.10).

name: Before creation: the Nāsadīya account

definitions.definition: Before creation there was neither non-being nor being, death nor immortality, night nor day; That One breathed windless by its own power; darkness hidden by darkness; That One was born by tapas; desire arose as the first seed of mind; seers found the bond of being in non-being in their hearts; the gods came later; whether even the overseer in the highest heaven knows is left open (RV 10.129).

members: the overseer who knows or does not know

name: The plurality of Vedic creation accounts

definitions.definition: The Saṃhitās give several accounts side by side: the Nāsadīya (10.129), the Puruṣa sacrifice (10.90), the Golden Germ (10.121), Viśvakarman the All-maker (10.81–82), Brahmaṇaspati smelting the worlds and being born from non-being (10.72), ṛta and satya from tapas (10.190), Vāc giving birth to the father (10.125.7), Indra's slaying of Vṛtra (1.32); in the Atharvaveda Skambha, Kāla, Kāma, Ucchiṣṭa, Virāj and Prāṇa.

Earth, atmosphere and heaven, formed from the Puruṣa's feet, navel and head (RV 10.90.14), each with its gods — Agni on earth, Vāyu or Indra in the atmosphere, Sūrya in heaven (Nirukta 7.5) — and named by the utterances bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ (VS 36.3).
The gods counted as eleven in heaven, eleven on earth and eleven in the waters (RV 1.139.11), or as 3,339 (3.9.9).

name: Time, the year and the wheel of ṛta

definitions.definition: The year is the twelve-spoked unaging wheel of ṛta with 720 sons (days and nights) (RV 1.164.11, 1.164.48); it was born from the ocean after ṛta and satya (10.190.2); the Disposer fashioned sun and moon 'as before' (10.190.3); generations pass while the dawns return (1.113.11); in the Atharvaveda Time itself is the first god (19.53–54).

Time is the seven-reined horse whose wheels are all beings; in Time are tapas, the eldest and brahman; Time is lord of all and father of Prajāpati; from Time arose the waters, brahman, tapas, the quarters and the Vedas (AVŚ 19.53–54).

The Earth is upheld by truth, order, consecration, tapas, brahman and sacrifice; she is mother and the speaker her son; she bears peoples of many speeches and dharmas; one digging her asks not to wound her vitals or heart (AVŚ 12.1).

Ṛta is the order by which the cosmos moves, the sacrifice succeeds and men act rightly; Agni is its guardian, Varuṇa and Mitra its lords; it was born with satya from tapas (RV 10.190.1); the year is its wheel (1.164.11); by it the Ādityas stand (10.85.1); with truth, consecration and tapas it upholds the earth (AVŚ 12.1.1).

relations.note: The ordinances (dharman, vrata) are the particular forms of the one order.

definitions.definition: Truth upholds the earth (RV 10.85.1); taking a vow, one goes 'from untruth to truth' (VS 1.5); Varuṇa's fetters bind the one who speaks untruth and release the truthful (AVŚ 4.16.6); Prāṇa places the truth-speaker in the highest world (11.4.11).

Dharman is what upholds: the first sacrifices were 'the first dharmas' (RV 10.90.16); the dead go to heaven and earth 'according to dharman' (10.16.3); men break the gods' dharmas through thoughtlessness (7.89.5); the Earth bears peoples of various dharmas (AVŚ 12.1.45).

name: Vrata: the gods' ordinance and the human vow

definitions.definition: Varuṇa is 'of firm ordinances' (RV 1.25); one prays to be sinless under his vrata (1.24.15); the sacrificer undertakes a vow before Agni, lord of vows (VS 1.5).

name: Varuṇa and Mitra, guardians of order

definitions.definition: Varuṇa, all-seeing sovereign, knows the paths of birds and ships and the months, is 'the third' when two conspire, counts the blinkings of men, and his spies never close their eyes; with Mitra he guards ṛta; he binds with fetters and releases.

Offence (āgas) and sin (enas) — one's own, done in the body, through wine, anger, dice or thoughtlessness, even in sleep, and those inherited from the fathers — bind as Varuṇa's fetters; the seer examines himself, asks the wise, confesses and asks to be loosened like a calf from its tether, to be sinless before Aditi (RV 1.24.15, 2.28.5, 5.85.7–8, 7.86–89).
The giver's wealth does not waste away; who eats alone has only sin (RV 10.117); givers of gifts stand high in heaven and partake of immortality (10.107.2).
Go together, speak together, let your minds know together (RV 10.191); 'I make you of one heart and mind, free from hatred' (AVŚ 3.30); may we look on all beings with the eye of a friend (VS 36.18).
Faith kindles the fire and makes the offering; it is invoked morning, noon and evening (RV 10.151); against doubters, 'have faith in him' (2.12.5).

Tapas is the heat by which That One was born (RV 10.129.3) and from which ṛta and satya came (10.190.1); by tapas the ancients reached heaven (10.154.2); the unheated do not attain soma (9.83.1); the student fills the worlds with tapas (AVŚ 11.5.4); the seers first undertook tapas and dīkṣā (19.41.1); Agastya's long tapas is set beside married life (RV 1.179).

name: The four varṇas in the Puruṣa Sūkta

definitions.definition: The brāhmaṇa was the Person's mouth, the rājanya his arms, the vaiśya his thighs; from his feet the śūdra was born (RV 10.90.12) — the one Saṃhitā verse naming the four varṇas together.

notes: Its later use and the debates about it are recorded in dsp:varna-origin-purusa-sukta.

name: A full life of a hundred autumns

definitions.definition: The ideal of a full human life: 'may we see, live, hear and speak a hundred autumns' (RV 7.66.16; VS 36.24); the living set a boundary against death and ask for long life (RV 10.18.4); rites for long life (AVŚ 8.1).

name: The person and the self in the Saṃhitās

definitions.definition: The person comprises body (tanū, śarīra), life-breath (asu, prāṇa), mind (manas), breath-self (ātman) and, in one reading, an 'unborn part' (RV 10.16.4); at death eye goes to the sun and breath to the wind (10.16.3); the immortal is of one origin with the mortal (1.164.30, 38); the seer does not know what he is (1.164.37) yet can say 'I was Manu and the Sun' (4.26.1); Sūrya is the self of all (1.115.1); the wise, ageless self is known without fear of death (AVŚ 10.8.44).

name: The two birds on one tree

definitions.definition: Two birds, companions, on one tree: one eats the sweet fig, the other looks on without eating (RV 1.164.20); the lord, guardian of the world, has entered 'me the simple one' (1.164.21).

notes: The Upaniṣads (Muṇḍaka 3.1.1, Śvetāśvatara 4.6) read the birds as the individual self and the Lord; the Ṛgveda does not name them.

definitions.definition: Mind is swiftest of flying things (RV 6.9.5), it wanders far and can be called back from Yama (10.58), it is yoked by the inspired (5.81.1; VS 11.1); the Śivasaṅkalpa verses call it the divine far-goer of waking and sleep, the one light of lights, knowing, thought and steadfastness, the immortal light within, holder of past, present and future, in which the Vedas are set and all thought woven, the heart-seated charioteer (VS 34.1–6); desire was its first seed (RV 10.129.4).
Dhī is the visionary thought the poets 'yoke' and fashion into hymns, which Savitṛ is asked to impel (RV 3.62.10, 5.81.1); with manīṣā in the heart the seers found the bond of being (10.129.4).

name: The heart as seat of inner seeing

definitions.definition: The seers searched in the heart (RV 10.129.4); a fixed light is set in the heart (6.9.5–6); the wise see with heart and mind (10.177.1); Vena saw the highest hidden in secret (VS 32.8); the mind is heart-seated (34.6).

name: Waking, sleep and dream in the Saṃhitās

definitions.definition: The mind goes far from the waking and likewise returns to the sleeper (VS 34.1); prāṇa stays awake upright among sleepers (AVŚ 11.4.25); Sleep (svapna) is 'neither living nor dead', child of Yama, and bad dreams are warded off (AVŚ 6.46); even sleep does not keep away wrong (RV 7.86.6).

notes: The Upaniṣadic scheme of three states and the fourth is contributed by U03; any correspondence is interpretive and not asserted here.

name: Desire as the first seed of mind

definitions.definition: Desire (kāma) arose in the beginning as the first seed of mind (RV 10.129.4; AVŚ 19.52.1).

name: Prāṇa, the life-breath, in the Saṃhitās

definitions.definition: Wind was born from the Puruṣa's breath (RV 10.90.13); Vāta is the breath of the gods, germ of the world (10.168.4); the Atharvaveda hails Prāṇa as lord of all, clothing creatures as a father his son, death and fever, the swan that never lifts one foot, awake among sleepers, bound to oneself for life (AVŚ 11.4).

name: The named breaths in the Saṃhitās

definitions.definition: The Saṃhitās name in-breath, out-breath and diffused breath (prāṇa, apāna, vyāna) with life (asu) among the goods of the Camaka (TS 4.7) and in long-life charms (AVŚ 8.1); the Vrātya has seven prāṇas, seven apānas and seven vyānas identified with fire, sun, moon, wind, waters, animals and creatures (AVŚ 15.15–17).

members: (udāna and samāna appear in later Vedic lists)

name: The body as the city of the gods

definitions.definition: The body is the eight-wheeled, nine-gated unconquerable stronghold of the gods with a golden sheath covered in light, in which dwells the self-possessed wonder (yakṣa) that the knowers of Brahman know; Brahman entered it; the person (puruṣa) is so called from this stronghold (pur) of Brahman (AVŚ 10.2.28–33); the nine-gated lotus covered with three strands holds the same yakṣa (10.8.43); all the gods dwell in the person as cows in a stall (11.8.32).

relations.note: The 'three strands' (guṇa) of AVŚ 10.8.43 are later read as the Sāṃkhya qualities; the verse itself does not define them — contested.

notes: Readings of 'eight wheels' as the body's centres (cakras) are later and interpretive; not asserted.

definitions.definition: Disease is caused by demons, worms, sorcery, the anger of gods, sin or inheritance, and is driven out by plants, waters, amulets, fire and sun, and by the healer's verses and touch; Rudra and the Aśvins are divine physicians; 'the waters are the remedy for all' (RV 10.137.6); the physician is one among whom plants gather (10.97.6).

name: Yajña: the sacrifice that sustains the world

definitions.definition: Ritual action is the Vedic paradigm of effective action: the gods first sacrificed the Person and 'sacrificed to the sacrifice with the sacrifice — these were the first dharmas' (RV 10.90.16); the sacrifice is woven like a cloth by the fathers (10.130.1); through it the petitions of the Camaka are 'made fit'.

name: Iṣṭāpūrta, merit of sacrifice and gift

definitions.definition: The merit of what one has sacrificed and given, with which the dead are reunited in the highest heaven (RV 10.14.8).

relations.note: Merit rejoins the dead in Yama's heaven.

name: The internalization of ritual (in its Saṃhitā beginnings)

definitions.definition: Already in the Saṃhitās the rite is referred beyond its outward form: the gods sacrificed the sacrifice (RV 10.90.16); the soma the brahmins know none eats (10.85.3); the first act of the fire-altar is the yoking of mind (VS 11.1); honouring a guest is itself the sacrifice (AVŚ 9.6); mind is the one in which the seven-hotṛ sacrifice is spread (VS 34.4).

notes: The fuller internalized rites (e.g. the prāṇāgnihotra of the Āraṇyakas) are U02's.

definitions.definition: Immortality is prayed for as full life and freedom from death (RV 7.59.12), won by soma ('we have become immortal', 8.48.3), by gifts (10.107.2), and as a place in the immortal world of light and bliss (9.113.7–11); 'knowing the Person one goes beyond death; there is no other path' (VS 31.18); 'knowing the ageless self one does not fear death' (AVŚ 10.8.44).

relations.note: Two strands: immortality as a heavenly world reached by rite and merit, and going beyond death by knowledge (VS 31.18; AVŚ 10.8.44).

name: The Vedic afterlife: Yama and the fathers

definitions.definition: The dead go by the ancient paths, past Yama's two four-eyed dogs, to Yama and the fathers in the highest heaven, where they are rejoined with their iṣṭāpūrta and a radiant body and rejoice in svadhā (RV 10.14); the fathers are lower, middle and higher (10.15.1); those who reached heaven by tapas, battle or great gifts are there (10.154); Kaśyapa asks for the immortal world of light and bliss (9.113).

name: The two paths: of the fathers and of the gods

definitions.definition: 'I have heard of two paths for mortals, of the fathers and of the gods' (RV 10.88.15); death is sent off by its own path, other than the path of the gods (10.18.1).

notes: The Upaniṣads (BĀU 6.2; ChU 5.10) develop the two paths; that development is U03's.

name: The funeral as the hymns present it

definitions.definition: The corpse is burned by Agni asked not to consume it utterly; eye goes to sun, breath to wind, limbs to plants and waters; the unborn part is carried to the world of the well-doers; the flesh-eating fire is sent away; the widow lying beside the dead is bidden to rise to the world of the living; the living set a boundary against death and go back to dancing and laughter; the bones are laid in mother earth (RV 10.16–18); the Atharvaveda includes those buried, cast out, burned and exposed (AVŚ 18.2.34).

Death has its own path (RV 10.18.1) and fetters (AVŚ 8.1.4); the mind can go to Yama and be called back (RV 10.58); 'let me not go to the house of clay' (7.89.1); one prays to be freed from death 'like a cucumber from its stalk, not from immortality' (7.59.12); the immortal and mortal are of one origin (1.164.30).

Speech is a goddess and cosmic power: she moves with all the gods, is queen and first of the worshipful, the power by which beings eat, see, breathe and hear, who makes whom she loves a seer (RV 10.125); she was found entered into the seers and reveals her body to some like a bride (10.71); gods begot her and animals speak her (8.100.11); the syllable in highest heaven bears the verses (1.164.39); she has four quarters, three hidden (1.164.45).

relations.note: The four quarters are the Saṃhitā's analysis of speech.

definitions.definition: Speech is measured in four quarters; the wise brahmins know them; three are hidden and do not stir; men speak the fourth (RV 1.164.45). The verse does not name them; the Nirukta records several readings (Oṃ and the three vyāhṛtis; noun, verb, preposition, particle; mantra, ritual text, brāhmaṇa and ordinary speech; ṛc, yajus, sāman and ordinary speech; speech of creatures; speech in the self), and later schools read the levels of speech.

relations.note: Grammarians and Kashmir Śaivas later read the four quarters as the levels of speech (vaikharī, madhyamā, paśyantī, parā) — an interpretive correspondence.

name: The ṛṣi as seer of the mantras

definitions.definition: The seers 'saw' the hymns and had direct perception of dharma, handing them on by instruction (Nirukta 1.20, 2.11); speech was found entered into the seers (RV 10.71.3); Vāc makes whom she loves a seer (10.125.5); Varuṇa made Vasiṣṭha a seer (7.88.4); the hymns also speak of being 'fashioned' by the poets (5.2.11).

Women are recorded as seers of Ṛgveda hymns and verses — Lopāmudrā, Ghoṣā, Apālā, Viśvavārā, Vāc Āmbhṛṇī, Śraddhā, Sūryā, Yamī, Indrāṇī, Śacī, Romaśā, Śaśvatī, Sārparājñī, Godhā, Agastya's sister and others — and listed together by the Bṛhaddevatā; the Atharvaveda says a maiden wins a husband by brahmacarya (AVŚ 11.5.18).

name: Transmission of the Veda: teacher, śākhā and oral recitation

definitions.definition: The Veda passes from the seers by instruction (Nirukta 1.20) to pupils who repeat the teacher's words (RV 7.103.5); the teacher initiates the student and bears him as an embryo (AVŚ 11.5.3); Vyāsa divided the one Veda into four and his pupils' lines branched into śākhās (Bhāgavata 1.4.19–23; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.4–5); each śākhā preserves its text by exact recitation.

name: The three Vedas (trayī) and the fourth

definitions.definition: From the Puruṣa sacrifice came the verses, chants, metres and formulas (RV 10.90.9); the ṛc is speech, the yajus mind, the sāman breath (VS 36.1); the older reckoning is the threefold Veda of the śrauta rite, to which the Atharvaveda is added as the fourth in the Purāṇic account of Vyāsa's division.

name: The Black and the White Yajurveda

definitions.definition: The Black (kṛṣṇa) Yajurveda mixes formulas and explanatory prose (Taittirīya, Maitrāyaṇī, Kāṭhaka, Kapiṣṭhala); the White (śukla) keeps the formulas (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā) apart from the Brāhmaṇa. The tradition tells that Yājñavalkya disgorged the Yajus learned from Vaiśampāyana, which his fellows took up as partridges (Taittirīya), and received new Yajus from the Sun as a horse (Vājasaneyi).

name: The recitation modes that guard the text

definitions.definition: The text is learned in the continuous form (saṃhitā), word by word (pada), in overlapping pairs (krama) and in the eight modified recitations (jaṭā, mālā, śikhā, rekhā, dhvaja, daṇḍa, ratha, ghana), with hand gestures marking the accents; understanding the meaning is also enjoined (Nirukta 1.18; Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 32–33, 54–55).

Vedic recitation distinguishes the raised (udātta), low (anudātta) and falling (svarita) accents; a mantra wrong in accent or letter does not convey its meaning and harms the sacrificer, as 'Indra-śatru' did (Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 52).

name: The Sāman notes and the musical scale

definitions.definition: The Sāmaveda sings with seven notes — kruṣṭa, prathama, dvitīya, tṛtīya, caturtha, mandra, atisvārya — which the Nāradīya Śikṣā sets against the flute's madhyama, gāndhāra, ṛṣabha, ṣaḍja, dhaivata, niṣāda and pañcama, places in the body from head to heart and shows on the fingers.

name: The parts of a sāman

definitions.definition: A sāman is a verse (from the ārcika) turned into song, with stretched vowels, repetitions and stobhas, divided among the chanters as hiṅkāra, prastāva, udgītha, pratihāra, upadrava and nidhana.

notes: The fivefold and sevenfold sāman are expounded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (U03).

definitions.definition: The metres (gāyatrī, triṣṭubh, jagatī, anuṣṭubh and others) were born from the Puruṣa sacrifice (RV 10.90.9) and are recorded for every verse in the Anukramaṇīs.

name: The muni and the long-haired one

definitions.definition: The wind-girdled munis in soiled brown, entered by the gods, ecstatic with munihood, ride the winds while mortals see only their bodies; the long-haired one bears fire, poison-drink and heaven and earth, flies through the air seeing all forms, knows the minds of beings and drank with Rudra (RV 10.136).

The student, initiated by the teacher who bears him as an embryo, fills the worlds with fuel, girdle, toil and tapas; by brahmacarya and tapas the king guards the realm, a maiden wins a husband and the gods struck down death (AVŚ 11.5).
